« Le silence des personnes blanches, c’e: “White silence is violence” read a sign carried by a white man at the Montréal demonstration held after the murder of George Floyd, who was asphyxiated under a police officer’s knee in Minneapolis. Since the death of the African American man, solidarity with Black people has grown around the world.
Le mot-clic #BlackLivesMatter est partou: The hashtag #BlackLivesMatter is everywhere on social media. But beyond social media, how can one be an ally to Black people? “I know people who appreciate it when their white friends post hashtags in solidarity on social media,” public relations specialist and columnist Martine St-Victor tells us. “For me, we need to take concrete action. I want a company to hire people from diverse backgrounds rather than post hashtags. But we live in a world where communication is about images, not substance,” she says.
Quelques heures avant la manifestation c: A few hours before the demonstration against police brutality in downtown Montréal, between two conference calls, amid a constant flow of people coming and going in her living room, Marlihan Lopez takes the time to have, for the umpteenth time, an educational discussion with a well-intentioned white journalist. In her view, the fact that racialized communities have to “educate” members of white communities so they can become better allies is an additional and unnecessary burden on racialized people. “This is a conversation you should be having among yourselves,” says the vice-president of the Fédération des femmes du Québec and coordinator at Concordia University’s Simone de Beauvoir Institute. “Police brutality is a phenomenon that affects Black and Indigenous people more, but solidarity is everyone’s work, and this conversation should involve all non-Black people,” she adds.
Être un allié, c’est plus que changer sa: Being an ally is more than changing your profile picture on social media. It is a process of learning and working on yourself that requires listening to people and educating yourself, she stresses. According to Ms. Lopez, one of the first things to do is to stop being so surprised. “We see a lot of shock among white people, but for us, it’s again and again and again,” she says, recalling the recent death of Regis Korchinski-Paquette, a Black woman from Toronto who died in circumstances that are still unclear, after falling from her balcony during a police intervention. “It’s happening with our neighbours to the south, but also with our neighbours, period,” says the academic coordinator.
« On n’a pas besoin de gens qui disent à: “We don’t need people who say every time, ‘I’m shocked’ or ‘I’m ashamed,’” Ms. Lopez continues. “People have to act. You have to listen, educate yourself and act according to your abilities.” And acting, she says, can take many forms: watching your friends’ kids while they go to a demonstration, calling out a relative who makes a racist comment, contacting your child’s school to demand an anti-racist curriculum, donating to a fundraising campaign, reading to better understand the racial dimension of migration or environmental issues, amplifying the message of an activist of colour instead of speaking on their behalf, and so on. “At some demonstrations in the United States, white people formed human chains. There are so many small things people can do, according to their abilities.”
De grandes choses sont également à faire: There are also big things to be done. Among them, obviously, is a rethinking of education. Webster, whose real name is Aly Ndiaye, is a musician, speaker and popularizer of history. For several years, he led guided tours of Old Quebec centred on the history of Black people in New France. Instead of telling the stories of Marguerite d’Youville and Samuel de Champlain, he talked about the lives of the slaves who worked for them and their associates – because, contrary to what Mr. Legault claimed at a press conference this week, there were indeed slaves in New France. “Understanding history allows you to understand where privilege comes from. The West’s economic supremacy is presented as something that happened by magic, but in reality, the place of Europe and the Americas in the world is a product of slavery and the massacre of Indigenous peoples.”
Webster nous invite à considérer l’histo: Webster invites us to consider “white” history from the perspective of Black and Indigenous people. Seen from an Indigenous perspective, this “noble” conquest becomes a terrifying genocide, a prelude to centuries of marginalization, he notes. Then he adds: “But even when [that perspective] is taught in schools, it isn’t given the same weight as the [white] perspective.” In his view, teaching more of the perspectives of Black and Indigenous people would have the effect of “recentring our understanding of citizenship.”
Mais une fois qu’on a refait nos cours d: But once we’ve redone our history classes, how do we act? Annette Henry, a specialist in whiteness and racism at the University of British Columbia, has a lot to say about the notion of the ally. “We don’t always pay attention to the words we use,” she says right off the bat. “People say, ‘I want to be an ally,’ but they don’t always know what that entails.”
Selon elle les bonnes intentions peuvent: In her view, good intentions can lead to the infantilization of the person one is trying to help or, worse, the re-creation of the power structures created by the omnipresence of privilege.
Elle note que les personnes qui s’adonne: She notes that people who engage in solidarity gain privileges from it, such as professional positions or social prestige. “Sometimes it’s more ‘palatable’ for a white person to hear other white people deliver these messages. People say, ‘They’re so brave to speak out!’ whereas we Black people talk about it with our colleagues every day! And they receive resources and accolades that should go to the people they are defending.”
« Nous vivons dans une société où les pe: “We live in a society where white people have certain privileges, and it’s a puzzle, because we don’t want to be treated as objects of charity.” By way of illustration, Professor Henry gives the comical example of a person who told her they would step aside from a position to offer it to her. “They were trying so hard to acknowledge their privilege that they ended up in absurdity.” When we spoke, she was drawing up a list of racialized candidates for the position of dean at UBC. “If you have access to certain networks, why not give someone a tap on the shoulder and say, ‘Why don’t you apply for this position? Why don’t you consider this person?’”
« Beaucoup de gens qui œuvrent dans les: “A lot of people who work in social justice spaces don’t pay us for our work and continue to benefit from systems and structures built on the backs of our ancestors,” Alishia McCullough and Jessica Wilson, two Black American health professionals and activists, sum up in an Instagram post. “They perpetuate this legacy by profiting from our voices and our experiences to increase their social capital and by using our knowledge, and then they put a price on their services. We need to demand accountability and make sure that, in the social justice world, people of colour are paid for what they do.”
Parfois, le geste de solidarité le plus: Sometimes the strongest act of solidarity is knowing when to give up the floor and learning, as an ally, to stop placing yourself at the centre of the story. Annette Henry cites the example of an Indigenous acquaintance who tried to dissuade a non-Indigenous researcher from attending a non-mixed meeting. “At some point, you have to be able to say to yourself, ‘I’m here in case someone needs me, but this isn’t my place.’ Some people are so used to being ‘central’ that they have trouble taking a few steps back.” She gives the example of a talk by journalist Desmond Cole at UBC where, during the question period, the organizers mainly gave the floor to racialized participants. “It can be hard for some people, but when you have participants who are so excited to see someone who looks like them… think about waiting before asking your question.”
Elle insiste non seulement sur l’écoute,: She insists not only on listening, but also on action. “People often want kits, ready-made solutions, but how is that going to help them have difficult conversations? They invited a Chinese person to their class to talk about their experience since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and she talked about it. Great. Now, what do they intend to do?” On June 1, Ms. Wilson and Ms. McCullough launched the Amplify Melanated Voices Challenge, which aims to give more visibility to engaged people of colour on social media. They suggest temporarily “muting” white people who create social justice content, and instead highlighting the contributions of racialized creators by sharing their work. They also invite all participants to reflect more deeply: “Think about how you see yourself, or don’t, reflected on social media… and consider how the predominant white perspective influences the way you view events. Then think about how this past week has been different for you, and what you took from it. Do you feel more informed? Did you understand something new? Are you uncomfortable?”
